description:
We are applying for retrospective planning permission for a timber decking of a pre-existing structure (world war 2 bunker underneath), a pergola and wooden fencing at the rear of our garden. 
Due to the safety risk of the open bunker for our children, we put wooden cladding around the bunker to create a terrace and built a very simple wooden pergola around it to enhance the privacy of the terrace through evergreen plants which are climbing up the pergola. We also built a boundary fence to the neighbour's garden to enhance privacy. 

When we moved into our house, the back of the garden was in a very poor state and badly maintained. As one progressed down to the back of the garden, the elevation increased due to an existing World War 2 concrete bunker, which was half raised out of the ground. 

Further to this, there was no boundary fence between our house and the house opposite (no. 16 Cranfield Road). Firstly, we agreed with the owners of no. 16, Mrs Lillalee Wright, to install a wooden fence – to provide both houses with more privacy.

We looked to resolve how best to deal with the remains of the existing concrete bunker  (please see accompanying pictures), that posed a health and safety risk for our two small children.

As we couldn’t move this concrete structure and it didn’t allow for any space for the planting of trees, we planned to build a wooden structure on top of the existing concrete structure, to make this part of the garden more usable, appealing and to help boost the biodiversity of the area.

We were notified that we needed planning permission for this (which we were not aware of) and had two pre-planning meetings (with Mr Max Curson). I will attach his response.

In response to the pre-planning meeting on 26th of April with Max Curson, we were given some feedback, which we have now implemented.

With regards to the height of the wooden decking (which is around 0.2m higher than the top of the bunker), it became apparent also to Mr Curson that given the uneven nature of the concrete structure, the decking could not feasibly be built on top of the structure at any lower a height. As such, the height of the decking is considered to be justified and non-excessive. 
The highest point of the decking is 1.044m above ground.

In order to prevent overlooking our neighbours’ garden from the raised decking, i.e. an issue of ensuring privacy, we have planted  three olive trees into the area between the decking and the fence. 
With regards to the privacy of our neighbours to the left (no 19) we have put planters all along the side and the front of the decking with screening plants.

This way, it was ensured that when we are on the decking, we won’t be able to look into any of our neighbours’ gardens.

We have discussed this plan with no 19 and 23 and they were happy for us to go ahead with this plan. 
In summary, Mr Curson communicated to us that what we had built was not at breach with any regulations or privacy issues
